key_terms.meaning: Controller output has only two states, fully ON or fully OFF, chosen by comparing the error with a fixed threshold.
Error band between the switch-ON and switch-OFF levels; a wider gap means a slower, larger output cycle.
Error range over which a P controller swings its output from minimum to maximum; PB = (100/Kp) percent of span.
Time in seconds in which the integral action repeats the present proportional output; larger Ti means weaker integral action.
Time in seconds by which derivative action leads a ramp; the D term is Kp·Td·de/dt.
Integral term keeps growing while the actuator is saturated, so the loop overshoots when the error finally falls.

key_terms.term: Ultimate gain Ku and ultimate period Pu
key_terms.meaning: Ku is the proportional gain at which the closed loop oscillates steadily; Pu is the period of that oscillation.
Open-loop step response of a first-order-plus-dead-time plant, from which gain K, dead time L and time constant T are read.
Gc(s) = Kc(1 + aTs)/(1 + Ts) with a > 1; its zero is nearer the origin than its pole, so it adds positive phase.
Peak phase of a lead network, reached at ωm = 1/(T√a); sin φm = (a − 1)/(a + 1).
Gc(s) = Kc(1 + Ts)/(1 + bTs) with b > 1; its pole is nearer the origin, so high-frequency gain is cut relative to low-frequency gain.
Ratio of high-frequency to low-frequency gain of a lag network; it fixes how much extra gain can be added without losing phase margin.
Two sections in cascade: the lag section raises low-frequency gain for accuracy, the lead section adds phase near crossover for stability.
Pick the compensator zero and pole so the compensated root locus passes through a chosen dominant closed-loop pole.
GM is the extra dB gain that drives |GH| to 1 at −180°; PM is the phase still in hand when |GH| = 1.
Seconds between two samples of the error in a digital controller; the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency.
Circuit after the DAC that keeps the controller output constant from one sample instant to the next.
Difference equation that outputs the change Δu(k) rather than u(k) itself, so saturation does not build up in the summer.

takeaways: On-off control is the cheapest controller but the output always cycles; the differential gap sets the size and speed of that cycle.
P action cuts rise time but leaves offset, I action removes offset but slows the loop, D action damps overshoot but amplifies noise.
Tuning rules such as Ziegler-Nichols convert two or three measured plant numbers into PID gains, giving a safe starting point that is then trimmed by hand.
A lead compensator adds phase near the gain crossover frequency, so phase margin and speed both go up, but high-frequency noise gets amplified.
A lag compensator keeps the gain high at low frequency and low at high frequency, which reduces steady-state error without giving up phase margin.
A lag-lead compensator is used when the plant needs both a large error constant and extra phase margin, which neither section can give alone.
Root-locus design places closed-loop poles where you want them; Bode design shapes gain and phase margins. Both realize lead and lag networks.
A digital PID is a difference equation run every T seconds, so the sampling period itself becomes a design parameter.
Always check the compensated design by simulation: margins and error constants are necessary targets, not proof of a good transient.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a short theory statement with a full worked design: state the specification, compute the compensator parameters, then verify phase margin or the error constant numerically.

bank.q: Draw and explain the response of a two-position controller driving a first-order plant. Show how the differential gap changes the amplitude and frequency of the resulting cycle.
outline: Block diagram of on-off controller plus plant
Output switches ON below (set point − gap/2) and OFF above (set point + gap/2)
Plant output is a sawtooth-like cycle about the set point
Wider gap gives larger amplitude but slower cycling
Ideal relay (zero gap) gives very fast switching, unrealisable in practice

bank.q: Explain the proportional, integral and derivative control actions. For each, state the effect on rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error.
outline: u(t) = Kp e + (Kp/Ti)∫e dt + Kp Td de/dt with each symbol defined
P: faster rise, offset remains, Kp too high causes oscillation
I: removes offset, adds a pole at origin, reduces stability margin
D: adds damping, reduces overshoot, amplifies high-frequency noise
Table of the four standard combinations P, PI, PD, PID

bank.q: Describe the Ziegler-Nichols continuous-cycling method and the process-reaction-curve method of PID tuning. Give the tuning formulas for P, PI and PID.
outline: Continuous cycling: raise Kp with I and D off until sustained oscillation, record Ku and Pu
Formulas: P Kp = 0.5Ku; PI Kp = 0.45Ku, Ti = Pu/1.2; PID Kp = 0.6Ku, Ti = Pu/2, Td = Pu/8
Reaction curve: record K, L, T from the open-loop step
Table using R = L/T; PID Kp = 1.2T/(KL), Ti = 2L, Td = 0.5L
Assumptions and limits: quarter-amplitude decay, model must be first order plus dead time

bank.q: Compare lead, lag and lag-lead compensators by pole-zero placement, Bode shape and the problem each one solves.
outline: Lead: zero closer to origin, phase bump, raises phase margin and bandwidth
Lag: pole closer to origin, high-frequency attenuation, raises low-frequency gain for a given margin, lowers error
Lag-lead: lag section at low frequency, lead section near crossover
Effect on rise time, overshoot and steady-state error for each
One-line rule for choosing among them

bank.q: A unity-feedback plant has G(s) = 40/(s(s+2)). Design a lead compensator so that the phase margin is at least 45° and the velocity error constant is unchanged.
outline: Find uncompensated PM and state the phase deficit
Choose α = (1 + sin φm)/(1 − sin φm) with φm = deficit + margin of safety
Place the zero at 1/(aT) one decade below the new crossover and pole at 1/T
Set Kc to keep Kv the same, since lead changes Kv by a
Recompute PM from the compensated Bode plot

bank.q: Design a lag compensator for G(s) = K/(s(s+1)(s+4)) so that the velocity error constant is 20 s⁻¹ and the phase margin is at least 40°.
outline: Set K to meet Kv = 20
Find the frequency where the uncompensated phase gives PM = 40° + 5° safety
Read the gain to be attenuated there, set b from it
Place the lag zero one decade below the new crossover, pole at zero/b
Choose Kc to restore the required Kv
Verify margins and error constant after compensation

bank.q: A plant G(s) = 10/(s(s+1)(s+5)) must have Kv = 100 s⁻¹ and phase margin of 45°. Design a lag-lead compensator and verify the result.
outline: Decide why one section is not enough: lag alone loses too much phase, lead alone cannot raise Kv
Lag section placed well below crossover to supply the gain
Lead section placed near crossover to supply phase
Combine the two transfer functions and set the overall gain
Check both Kv and PM, then sketch the compensated Bode plot

bank.q: An open-loop step test on a process gives gain K = 2, dead time L = 1 s and time constant T = 4 s. Find P, PI and PID settings by the Ziegler-Nichols reaction-curve rules.
outline: Write the first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = Ke^(−Ls)/(Ts+1)
Compute R = L/T = 0.25
Apply the tabulated formulas for Kp, Ti, Td
Give the resulting transfer function of the controller
Mention that plant tests must be done near the operating point

bank.q: A digital PID controller runs at T = 0.1 s with Kp = 2, Ti = 1 s and Td = 0.05 s. Write the positional and velocity difference equations for the control signal.
outline: Sampled error e(k), integral replaced by T·Σe(j), derivative by (e(k) − e(k−1))/T
Substitute numbers to get u(k)
Velocity form Δu(k) = u(k) − u(k−1)
Explain why the velocity form avoids windup and gives bumpless transfer
Compute u(k) for two or three sample values

bank.q: An on-off controller with a differential gap of ±0.5 °C switches a heater for an oven modelled as a first-order plant. Estimate the cycle amplitude and period of the temperature.
outline: Two-position control gives ON below lower threshold, OFF above upper threshold
Write heating and cooling exponentials between the limits
Cycle amplitude equals the gap plus the overshoot caused by plant lag
Period from the time constants of the two exponentials
State how smaller gap or larger plant delay changes the period

bank.q: Compare the root-locus and the Bode-plot methods of compensator design. State the information each gives and the situations in which each is the easier tool.
outline: Root locus: works directly with closed-loop pole positions and damping ratio
Bode: works with margins, bandwidth and error constants read from the plot
Lead and lag can be designed by either route, with different parameter choices
Root locus is easier for specifying damping and settling time; Bode for robustness margins
Both are models, so a final simulation is needed

bank.q: A lead-compensated loop becomes noisy and the actuator chatters. Analyse the cause and discuss at least three remedies.
outline: Lead network boosts the loop gain at high frequency
Derivative action further amplifies measurement noise
Remedy one: lower the maximum phase lead or move the network to lower frequency
Remedy two: use a filtered derivative, Td/(1 + sTd/N)
Remedy three: measure with a smoother sensor or add a low-pass filter outside the loop
Trade-off: less noise but lower phase margin

bank.q: Discuss how the choice of sampling period affects a digital PID controller. Include computation load, aliasing, quantisation and stability.
outline: Shannon limit: sampling rate above twice the highest signal frequency
Too large T: aliasing, extra phase lag from the zero-order hold, possible instability
Too small T: more computation, noise in the differencing term, coefficient rounding
Rule of thumb of 10 to 30 samples per closed-loop rise time
Effect on the equivalent continuous gains and on Ti, Td in samples

bank.q: For a home water heater and a DC motor speed drive, choose between on-off control and PID control. Justify each choice using cost, accuracy, actuator life and dynamic behaviour.
outline: Water heater: large thermal lag, no need for fine accuracy, on-off with hysteresis keeps the contactor from wearing out
Motor drive: needs accurate, fast speed holding, so PI or PID is chosen
Steady-state error requirement decides whether integral action is needed
Actuator wear and switching frequency as a real design constraint
Cost and complexity of the controller as the final trade-off

glossary.def: The value the controlled variable should have.
Set point minus measured output, e(t) = r(t) − y(t), the input to the controller.
Control in which the actuator has only two positions, fully ON or fully OFF.
Range of error over which a controller makes no change in output.
Deliberate difference between the error level that turns the output ON and the level that turns it OFF.
Steady-state error left by proportional-only control.
Percentage of the input span over which a proportional controller output travels its full range.
Growth of the integral term during actuator saturation, which delays recovery and causes overshoot.
Sudden jump in controller output when the set point is stepped, caused by differentiation of the error.
Switching a controller between manual and automatic without a jump in the actuator signal.
Proportional gain at which a closed loop under P control oscillates with constant amplitude.
Period of the sustained oscillation at the ultimate gain.
Open-loop response of a plant to a step input, used to extract gain, delay and time constant.
A network or algorithm added to a loop to improve its steady-state accuracy or its transient response.
Frequency at which the open-loop magnitude equals 1, or 0 dB.
Frequency at which the open-loop phase equals −180°.
180° plus the open-loop phase at the gain crossover frequency.
Factor, or its decibel value, by which the gain can rise before the loop becomes unstable.
Device that holds a sampled value constant until the next sample arrives.
A high-frequency signal appearing as a false low frequency because the sampling rate is too low.
Time interval T between two successive samples in a digital controller.
Recurrence relation that computes the present control output from present and past samples.
The pair of closed-loop poles closest to the imaginary axis, which sets the visible transient.
A compensator placed in series with the plant, ahead of the summing junction's forward path.
